overview: The Petun, also called Tionontati, were Iroquoian-speaking communities south of Georgian Bay. The map’s 1492 to 1500 label is earlier than the well-documented Petun villages discussed here, which developed in the late 1500s and 1600s. Archaeologists debate their earlier origins. Their descendants helped form later Wyandot communities; this early map cutoff is not their disappearance.

periods.title: Villages south of Georgian Bay
periods.summary: Archaeology traces communities into their historic region during the late sixteenth century.

periods.title: Missions, trade and upheaval
periods.summary: The documented village network experienced growing contact, refugee arrivals and attack.

periods.title: Wyandot communities
periods.summary: Survivors formed new communities with people of other Iroquoian backgrounds.

items.text: Researchers associate the historic Petun with two groupings conventionally called Wolf and Deer. Their earlier origins are debated: proposals connect them with communities in the Humber Valley or farther southwest in Neutral country. Pottery connections help investigate movement, but do not turn either proposed route into a certainty.

Charles Garrad noticed that several Petun village sites occur in pairs: a larger settlement close to a smaller one. The Deer settlements were especially close together. He interpreted these patterns as relationships between communities with different functions, rather than assuming every cluster of houses operated independently.

Garrad proposed that some smaller settlements accommodated visitors, including Odawa people who spent winters among the Petun. Different artifact and animal-bone patterns supported his investigation. This offers a picture of villages with guests and seasonal connections, while the exact role of each settlement remains a research question.

When Champlain visited in January 1616, he described people growing maize and living in permanent settlements. His hosts supplied meat and fish for a feast during his visits among neighboring villages. The account connects farming with hospitality: welcoming travelers meant sharing a meal as well as discussing friendship.

At Plater-Fleming, copper-kettle fragments were plentiful while pottery was comparatively scarce. Garrad interpreted this as evidence that imported kettles had replaced some clay cooking vessels at that particular late Petun settlement. Changes in trade could therefore alter the objects used to prepare everyday food.

Glass beads also help investigate Plater-Fleming’s date. Its small recorded assemblage included red tubular beads, a style useful for comparison with other late contact-period sites. A bead was an ornament to its owner; centuries later, its material and shape also help archaeologists compare settlements.

Animal remains make beaver processing particularly visible at Petun sites. Garrad compared bone assemblages from named villages and found beaver among the most common identified mammals. Those remains record intensive work with animals linked to the fur trade; percentages of bones are not percentages of people’s dinner.

Modern experiments by J. Allan Blair tested whether native tobacco could grow near old village sites. Carefully weeded and fenced plants matured, while open-field plantings failed. The experiment highlights the effort of protecting young plants from weeds and hungry animals, without proving exactly how every Petun garden was arranged.

The Wyandotte Nation explains that the Tionontati were separate from the old Huron-Wendat confederacy. They received refugees, then suffered Haudenosaunee attacks. Survivors joined with Attignawantan and Wenro people in 1649 and 1650, forming a new community while drawing on several earlier identities.

The modern Wyandotte Nation’s shield recalls twelve clans, including several turtle clans as well as Wolf, Bear and Deer. These names form part of the Nation’s own account of family and community identity today; the shield is not a diagram of the earlier Petun village map.

A short modern Waⁿdat example is “aža?áha,” meaning “she is a child.” Beci Wright printed it in the Wyandotte Nation’s newspaper in August 2022, with linguistic support credited to Craig Kopris. This sample belongs to a descendant community’s language teaching, rather than an unchanged sentence documented in Petun country in 1492.

That 2022 language column paired written examples with audio recordings and invited learners to online practice sessions. Children, elders and adults appeared together in its vocabulary of age. A modern classroom can reach families living far apart, helping language learning fit into ordinary community life.

The same newspaper invited artists to a 2022 community showcase with separate youth and adult divisions. Categories included beadwork, pottery, basketry, textiles and mixed media. Younger artists could show their work alongside older makers, giving creativity and shared learning a place in the gathering.

ending.text: Attacks dispersed Petun communities in 1649 and 1650. Survivors helped form the later Wyandot people, whose communities continue. Political upheaval and new shared identities, rather than extinction at the map’s 1500 cutoff, explain this transition.
